slides.title: What drove the decline
Gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment, not wages, explain 79% of the margin decline since FY2023

claims.claim: 79% of the 2.35-percentage-point fall came from gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment
evidence: Chart: Operating margin FY2023 3.37%; Gross margin step 1.02 pp; E-commerce fulfillment 0.84 pp; Store labor 0.30 pp; Occupancy and energy 0.20 pp; FY2025 1.02%
Other SG&A held at 4.7% of sales and is left out; steps sum to the change within rounding

claims.claim: Gross margin: the largest step, driven by deeper promotions and higher shrink
E-commerce fulfillment: up from 0.4% to 1.2% of sales as online orders nearly tripled and more went to the home
Store labor: only 13% of the decline, although it is the focus of the draft plan

slides.title: Promotions and shrink, both within Harlow's control, explain the whole fall in gross margin since FY2023

claims.claim: Each driver has an operating cause Harlow can act on
evidence: Chart: change in gross margin, pp of sales: Promotional mix -0.7; Shrink -0.5; Private-label mix +0.18
Together the three equal the 1.02 pp fall in gross margin

claims.claim: Promotional mix: promoted sales rose from 24.0% to 29.0% of sales, and each dollar earns 14 percentage points less margin
Less vendor support: suppliers funded 46% of markdowns in FY2025, down from 55%, so Harlow carries more of each event
Shrink: up from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales while hours per $1,000 of sales fell
Private-label mix: share up from 17.0% to 18.5% of sales at 12 percentage points more margin, the one driver working for Harlow

slides.title: Wage inflation was largely absorbed by productivity, leaving store labor only 0.3 percentage points of sales higher

claims.claim: 9.4% rise in the average hourly wage incl. benefits, in line with the CFO's "more than 9%"
evidence: State minimum wage and a tight labor market
Set outside Harlow; a further 4% rise is due in 2027

claims.claim: −6% change in labor hours per $1,000 of sales offset most of the wage rise
evidence: Hours already grew more slowly than sales
The thinnest-staffed stores now skip produce rotation and receiving checks

claims.claim: 0.3 pp change in store labor as a share of sales: 13% of the fall in operating margin
evidence: Wage rise net of productivity
Smaller than the 0.84-percentage-point rise in e-commerce fulfillment

slides.title: The draft labor cut
Thinly staffed stores already lose the most to shrink: 3.1% of sales, against 2.3% in the best-staffed quartile

claims.claim: Fewer hours mean skipped checks on fresh food
evidence: Chart: shrink % of sales FY2025: Fewest hours (Q1) 3.1%; Q2 2.7%; Q3 2.4%; Most hours (Q4) 2.3%; Chain average 2.6%

claims.claim: Fewest hours (Q1): these stores lose 35% more of their sales to shrink than the best-staffed quartile
Why: their managers say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days
Exposed: fresh and produce waste (45%) and receiving errors (20%) make up 65% of shrink, both tied to staff time
Over time: chain hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6.0% in FY2023–25 while shrink rose from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales

slides.title: The draft hour cut could net as little as $4.5M of its $14.5M saving once higher shrink is counted

claims.claim: The draft hour cut could net as little as $4.5M of its $14.5M saving
evidence: $14.5M saving a year, management's estimate
− $10M more shrink a year: 0.67 percentage points of sales if shrink tracks hours as in FY2023–25
= $4.5M net saving a year, before lost sales from checkout waits or stock-outs

claims.claim: A cut treats a minor cause of the decline and feeds a major one: move hours to the high-shrink stores instead

slides.title: Promotions, shrink and private label
Deeper promotions have not paid off, with 38% of FY2025 events losing money and price perception getting worse

claims.claim: Promotions grew to 29% of sales in two years
evidence: +5 pp
Promotional share: FY2023 24%; FY2024 26.2%; FY2025 29%

claims.claim: Yet more customers now find Harlow expensive
evidence: +8 pp
Say Harlow is more expensive than other options: FY2023 33%; FY2025 41%, n = 3,100

claims.claim: And many events lose money outright
evidence: 38% of FY2025 events lost money, extra units counted
Vendor funding 46%, from 55%
Set to defend against ValuMart

claims.claim: The category team's case (1.8% compared with 0.2% comparable-sales growth in the deepest-promotion stores) counts sales, not profit

slides.title: Resetting promotions is the largest gross-margin action, worth about $10.5M a year

claims.claim: Promotions first: largest, and acts within months
evidence: Chart: operating income added a year, $M: Promotions back to 24% of sales 10.521; Shrink down to 2.3% of sales 4.509; Private label at FY2023–25 pace 4.0581

claims.claim: Promotions: 5 percentage points of sales back to regular price, each dollar earning 14 percentage points more margin; drop money-losing events first
Shrink: from 2.6% to the best quartile's 2.3% of sales by moving hours to receiving and produce rotation
Private label: 0.75 percentage points of share a year for three years, at 12 percentage points more margin
$19.1M operating income a year, before one-time costs
evidence: 1.3 pp of sales (promotions 0.7, shrink 0.3, private label 0.3) × $1,503M FY2025 sales = $19.1M

claims.claim: Risk: stores within three miles of a ValuMart had comparable sales of −4.2%, against +1.1% elsewhere; hold their key prices

slides.title: E-commerce loses about $10M a year in full; the tested delivery fee cuts that by $2.8M
Counted in full, e-commerce loses about $10M a year instead of earning the 6.1% margin reported to the board

claims.claim: 6.1% contribution margin on e-commerce sales, as reported by the e-commerce team
evidence: About $7.8M on $127.8M of online sales
Leaves out third-party delivery, which finance books in fulfillment
Treats every online sale as new to Harlow

claims.claim: −$10.4M contribution a year once delivery and store cannibalization are counted
evidence: $127.8M e-commerce sales (8.5% of sales) × 30% new to Harlow; 70% would have been bought in store (n = 2,300) × 20 cents of contribution per new dollar (finance) − $18.1M fulfillment, net of delivery fees = −$10.4M contribution a year
Delivery costs $13.80 per delivered order, against an average fee of $3.10
58% of orders now go to the home, up from 45% in FY2023

claims.claim: Freezing e-commerce at today's size, as the draft plan proposes, keeps this loss

slides.title: Rolling out the tested delivery fee would cut the e-commerce loss by about $2.8M a year and keep home delivery

claims.claim: $2,844K gain a year; the loss falls to about $7.6M
evidence: $2,103K more fee income: 703k delivered orders at $6.40, against 772k at $3.10
+ $959K less delivery cost: 9% fewer delivered orders at $13.80
− $65K more picking as click-and-collect orders rise 14%
− $153K contribution lost on 2% lower online sales

claims.claim: The test was small, so the rollout should be staged and tracked
evidence: 4-store, 10-week test

claims.claim: Delivery still loses money: about $9.04 per delivered order at the tested fee, against $1.64 for click-and-collect
Use the contract renewal to resist the 3% rate rise: the fee alone does not make delivery pay
evidence: the provider's proposed 3% rise would cost about $0.3M a year

slides.title: Plan and first actions
Exiting the six loss-making stores whose leases end by 2027 adds about $4.4M a year at no exit cost

claims.claim: Six stores, leases end by 2027: act at lease end; no vote and no exit cost
evidence: Operating income gain $4.4M a year; one-time exit cost None; sales lost to Harlow $59M a year; board vote Not needed

claims.claim: Three stores, leases run beyond 2027: payback of 3.4 years ($7.5M against $2.2M a year)
evidence: Operating income gain $2.2M a year; one-time exit cost $7.5M; sales lost $29.5M a year; board vote Required

claims.claim: All nine stores: needed to reach 3.0%
evidence: Operating income gain $6.6M a year; one-time exit cost $7.5M; sales lost $88.5M a year; board vote for three stores
$3.1M four-wall EBITDA loss removed + $3.5M (25% of $118.0M sales move to nearby stores at 12% contribution) = $6.6M a year for all nine

slides.title: Together, six actions would lift operating income to about $44M, a 3.1% margin on FY2025 sales

claims.claim: Six actions lift operating income to about $44M, a 3.1% margin
evidence: Chart: FY2025 15.3; Promotions +10.521; Delivery fee +2.844; Shrink +4.509; Private label +4.0581; Six store exits +4.4267; Three store exits +2.2133; After plan 43.8721 ($M)
3.1%: $43.9M ÷ $1,412M of sales after exits and lost online sales

claims.claim: The first three actions clear the covenant
evidence: promotions, the delivery fee and shrink add about $17.9M, taking operating income to $33.2M against the $20M floor

claims.claim: Board vote: without the three long-lease exits the margin would be about 2.9%
Thin headroom: about $1.5M above 3.0%; a 4% rise on the whole store-labor bill would cost $7.3M
Not counted: vendor funding back toward 55% and a lower delivery rate

slides.title: Unlike the draft plan, ours keeps store hours and targets the real causes: promotions, shrink, delivery and weak stores

claims.claim: Diagnosis: draft says wage inflation is the main cause; recommended: gross margin and e-commerce cause 79% of the decline
evidence: Store labor explains 13%

claims.claim: Store hours: draft cuts scheduled hours by 8%; recommended keeps hours and moves them to the high-shrink stores
evidence: The cut's net saving could fall to about $4.5M

claims.claim: Promotions: not addressed in draft; recommended cut money-losing events until promotions are 24% of sales
evidence: About $10.5M a year

claims.claim: Private label: not addressed in draft; recommended keep adding 0.75 percentage points of share a year
evidence: About $4.1M a year

claims.claim: E-commerce: draft freezes at current size; recommended roll out the tested fee and steer orders to click-and-collect
evidence: Loss falls from about $10.4M to $7.6M a year

claims.claim: Stores: not addressed in draft; recommended exit the nine loss-making stores, six at lease end
evidence: About $6.6M a year for $7.5M one-time

slides.title: Promotions, the delivery fee and shrink go first: they act within FY2026 and alone clear the lender's covenant

claims.claim: Timeline H1 FY2026 to FY2028: Promotions (drop money-losing events; reopen vendor funding), Delivery fee (staged fee rollout; steer orders to click-and-collect), Shrink (move hours to receiving and produce rotation), Private label (add 0.75 pp of share a year), Store exits (six stores as leases end; three long-lease stores)
evidence: Milestones: Board vote on three exits; 3.0% margin; Covenant test

claims.claim: Decision today: approve the six actions, including three long-lease exits at $7.5M of the $25M limit

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Decision today: approve the six actions, including three long-lease exits at $7.5M of the $25M limit. Harlow should fix promotions, shrink and delivery and exit weak stores, not cut store hours; promotions, the delivery fee and shrink go first.

alternatives_considered.option: Draft plan (CFO and COO): cut scheduled store hours by 8%
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: could net as little as $4.5M of its $14.5M saving once higher shrink is counted; "A cut treats a minor cause of the decline and feeds a major one: move hours to the high-shrink stores instead"; next step: cancel the 8% hour cut.

alternatives_considered.option: Draft plan: freeze e-commerce at current size
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: "Freezing e-commerce at today's size, as the draft plan proposes, keeps this loss"; instead roll out the tested fee and steer orders to click-and-collect.

alternatives_considered.option: Exit only the six stores whose leases end by 2027
alternatives_considered.treatment: Act at lease end, no vote and no exit cost, $4.4M a year; but without the three long-lease exits the margin would be about 2.9%.

alternatives_considered.option: Exit the three stores whose leases run beyond 2027
alternatives_considered.treatment: Board vote required; $7.5M one-time cost, payback of 3.4 years; recommended as needed to reach 3.0%.
Chosen: $6.6M a year for $7.5M one-time; needed to reach 3.0%.

alternatives_considered.option: Category team's case for deep promotions
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: its 1.8% vs 0.2% comparable-sales growth in the deepest-promotion stores "counts sales, not profit".

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Synthetic benchmark data; every figure from the briefing pack
Other SG&A held at 4.7% of sales and is left out; steps sum to the change within rounding. Fiscal years end in January
The pack gives shrink by quartile but not each quartile's hours or sales

Hour cut: shrink responds to hours as it did in FY2023–25, when hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6.0% and shrink rose 0.5 percentage points; all of that rise is put down to staffing, which makes this an upper bound
Hour cut: the saving is management's estimate of $14.5M a year, close to 8% of FY2025 store labor of $181.9M
Hour cut: sales stay at the FY2025 level of $1,503M
Hour cut: lost sales from longer checkout waits and stock-outs are not counted; they would lower the net saving further
Risk: stores within three miles of a ValuMart had comparable sales of −4.2%, against +1.1% elsewhere; hold their key prices
Sales that move online from a store are assumed to earn the same contribution either way, before fulfillment
Delivery fee: the 4-store, 10-week test holds chain-wide: delivered orders −9%, click-and-collect +14%, online sales −2%, fee $6.40
Delivery fee: costs per order stay at FY2025 rates; the provider's proposed 3% rise would cost about $0.3M a year
Delivery fee: lost online sales follow the survey: 70% move to Harlow stores and 30% leave Harlow
The test was small, so the rollout should be staged and tracked
Store-level figures are not in the pack, so six and three stores are pro-rated from the nine-store totals
Thin headroom: about $1.5M above 3.0%; a 4% rise on the whole store-labor bill would cost $7.3M
No wage, rent or delivery-rate inflation and no sales growth assumed
Not counted: vendor funding back toward 55% and a lower delivery rate
We read FY2026 as the fiscal year that starts after the February 2027 meeting
next_steps: Stop the money-losing promotional events and reopen vendor-funding talks with the top suppliers — Chief merchant and category managers — Q1 FY2026
Roll out the $7.99 fee and $100 threshold in stages, tracking orders and sales weekly; push back on the 3% rate rise — E-commerce lead and procurement — Q1 FY2026
Cancel the 8% hour cut; move hours to receiving and produce rotation in the thinnest-staffed stores — COO — Q1 FY2026
Plan exits of the six stores at lease end; bring the three long-lease exits to a board vote — CFO and real estate — Q2 FY2026
Report margin, shrink and covenant headroom to the board every quarter — CFO — From Q2 FY2026
normalized.extraction_notes: The deck came as plain text with no images. I read the chart values from the [Chart] series data. On slide 4 the waterfall step sizes come from the 'Operating margin' series, and the 'base' series is spacing for the waterfall. I paired the Gantt bars on slide 20 with their rows by the order they appear, because the text gives no exact timing for each bar. Slide 13's section-divider subtitle says only "E-commerce", and its title repeats executive-summary point 4.
